The inhabitants, calling themselves the Citizens of the Hollow Frame, have declared themselves neutral in all earthly conflicts, devoted instead to the preservation of obsolete film formats and the ethical treatment of analog memory. They hold evening assemblies in the old projection booth, where flickering shadows and forgotten reels serve as both entertainment and philosophical guideposts. 

Above them, the world continues to function in its accustomed way, though with increasing dissonance. Politicians speak in broader and broader brushstrokes to mask the erosion of meaning. Reporters ask the same questions louder. And somewhere, in the vast infrastructure of unacknowledged collapse, someone is already working on a new term to describe what comes next.

In the quiet annals of bureaucratic absurdity, there exists a department known only as the Bureau of Atmospheric Nomenclature. Its mission: to classify the precise emotional resonance of each weather pattern, assigning them poetic titles suitable for public broadcast. The work is delicate, demanding both meteorological expertise and a flair for metaphor, and though the general populace remains largely unaware of the bureau’s existence, they benefit daily from its labors. When thunderstorms roll in, they are no longer simply “severe weather events,” but “Crescendos of the Skies.” When the sun breaks through a lingering gloom, it is not just clearing skies—it is the “Awakening of the Amber Sovereign.”

Established in 1943 under President Franklin Delano Roosevelt as a morale-boosting measure during the height of the war, the bureau grew slowly at first, adding one poeticist and three climatographers before the end of the decade. By the 1960s, it had expanded across three floors of a modest federal building in Des Moines. Its influence was subtle but profound; the way people spoke of rain, of fog, of wind, subtly shifted in tone. A child might say, “It’s raining today,” but after the Bureau’s intervention, the same child might say, “The tears of the heavens are falling this afternoon.”

Each year, the Bureau hosts a symposium where poets, scientists, and philosophers gather to debate the semantics of storms and the sonnets hidden in snowfall. The most anticipated event is the annual Best Title ceremony, where a new name is bestowed upon a recently identified pattern of cloud formations, barometric pressure shifts, or atmospheric inversions. Last year, a rare form of twilight haze that appeared only in the Pacific Northwest was named “Mourning Mantle of the Cascades,” a phrase so hauntingly beautiful that it entered the vernacular of local newspapers and coffee shop baristas alike.

But the Bureau faces challenges. Budget cuts. Technological skepticism. The rise of data-driven language, stripped of sentiment. Some lawmakers now question whether assigning poetry to the sky is a frivolous expenditure in times of fiscal austerity. The director, Dr. Thalia Marnwell, a former bard and now a woman in her sixties with spectacles and a penchant for metaphor, argues that weather is not just a function of temperature and pressure—it is a narrative. And narratives, she insists, deserve names.

THE latest breakthrough in artificial affectivity is the QX-9 Emotional Resonance Unit, a sleek, egg-shaped device roughly the size of a cantaloupe, though significantly easier to carry. Unlike prior models, the QX-9 does not merely mimic emotional states; it *responds* to them. Placed within ten feet of a human subject, it adjusts its internal tonality and color spectrum according to the wearer’s fluctuating mood—pulsing soft blues for melancholy, bright golds for contentment, and deep crimson if the subject is even slightly annoyed. But the QX-9 goes beyond reflection. It harmonizes. Users report, in clinical studies and casual testimonials alike, that their moods begin to align with the device, as if the machine is not just mirroring emotion, but gently guiding it.

Developed in a joint effort between NeuraTech Industries and the Institute for Sentient Algorithmic Development, the QX-9 was initially marketed as a tool for corporate wellness. Employees experiencing stress, it was claimed, could reset their internal rhythms simply by placing the device on their desk. The results, according to the company’s internal tracking logs, were “statistically significant and aesthetically pleasing.” Within a year, the QX-9 had moved from conference rooms to living rooms. It was no longer seen as a tool, but a companion. Some users began calling it "The Mood Egg."

Among the most vocal advocates was Margaret Tillinghast, a school administrator from Davenport, Iowa, who claimed that her QX-9 had saved her marriage. “I used to come home exhausted,” she told a local talk show. “But the moment I walked through the door, my unit would shift to a gentle lavender. I'd breathe. I'd relax. And instead of yelling at the kids about their homework, I'd sit down and read with them.”

Not everyone was convinced.

Dr. Leonard Kessler, a cognitive ethicist from the University of [REDACTED], issued a public statement warning against the long-term psychological effects of external emotional modulation. “If we outsource our emotional regulation to a machine,” he said during a televised debate, “we risk becoming dependent—not just on the device, but on the algorithm that guides it. What happens when we forget how to feel without it?”

He was ignored.

By the end of the year, over 12 million QX-9 units had shipped. Sales were projected to hit 25 million by Q1 next fiscal cycle. One user, a man named Thomas Granger from Salt Lake City, wrote a touching letter to the company:

“I've never felt so understood,” he wrote. “Like someone finally *gets* me, even when I don’t get myself.”

No one ever told him that the QX-9 didn't understand anything at all.

The latest proposal for the Strategic Defense Initiative, code-named *Aegis Ascendant*, has stirred both fervor and consternation among the architects of national security, as well as those who prefer their peace with a little less posturing. At the heart of the plan is a constellation of automated, laser-armed satellites intended to intercept incoming threats—nuclear, biological, ideological—before they touch foreign soil or national sensibilities. The project’s proponents, speaking in tones somewhere between evangelism and bureaucratic bravado, insist that *Aegis Ascendant* is not merely the future of defense but a necessary reckoning with the past: a rejection of static, vulnerable silos, of the cold, entrenched logic of mutual assured destruction.

“This is no longer the arms race,” declared Dr. Marlene Voss, Chief Technologist of the National Defense Authority, at a press conference staged in a glass-walled atrium that offered an ironic view of the very missiles her satellites might one day neutralize. “This is the shield race. And we must move ahead with clarity and urgency.” She spoke with the conviction of someone who had long since stopped listening to the doubters—those who questioned the cost, the feasibility, or the moral implications of militarizing space. To her, *Aegis* was both a necessity and a testament to progress, a shining answer to the question of how a modern democracy protects itself in an age of shadow warfare and existential anxiety.

Yet behind the confident rhetoric, fractures were forming. Among defense contractors, there was an uneasy acknowledgment that the *Aegis* system was still more theory than reality—a collection of prototypes, simulations, and optimistic projections. Some officials, less enamored with metaphors about invincibility, wondered aloud whether the initiative would be more effective as a symbol than as a weapon. Others, in whispered conversations over lukewarm coffee and encrypted memos, speculated that the real function of *Aegis* was not so much to defend as to deter, not to destroy but to display dominance.

And then there were the critics from outside the corridors of power—academics, activists, and a few weary former generals—who saw in *Aegis Ascendant* not a leap forward but a dangerous doubling down on the same cycle of escalation that had defined so much of the twentieth century. “Every time we build a wall,” one commentator wrote, “we forget that walls don’t keep enemies away—they just give us more reason to fear them.”

For now, the debate raged in headlines and hearings, in think tank briefings and late-night cable segments. But beneath the noise, the work continued. Satellites were being tested, lasers calibrated, orbits charted. And in the hushed chambers of leadership, decisions were being made—not just about the fate of a system, but about the shape of the world that system might create.

IN the year of our Lord 1989, shortly after the fall of the Berlin Wall and just before the rise of the World Wide Web, a certain brand of desk calendar gained cult status among mid-level managers, retired schoolteachers, and the elderly. The calendar in question was not notable for its holidays or even its weather forecasts, but for the way it handled the weekends: instead of the usual blanks or vague suggestions for leisure (“Relax!”, “Read!”, “Sleep!”), the calendar offered actual activities, complete with phone numbers, times, and a stern moral imperative. 

Each Saturday and Sunday, in elegant block letters, it would advise: “Attend the 10:00 AM Service at St. Agnes’” or “Call Your Elderly Parent” or “Donate Blood at Mercy Hospital.” Not “consider donating blood,” mind you—“Don’t Be Lazy. Do It.” And so, with remarkable regularity, the citizens of Midvale, Ohio, did.

The calendar had been designed by a former typesetter named Marvin Dole, a widower in his late sixties who had spent thirty-two years aligning text on pages before retiring early due to a case of carpal tunnel he never quite explained. Marvin, who lived alone in a split-level house with a cat named Montezuma, had grown tired of the passive-aggressive tone of modern life—posters urging you to “just say no,” toasters that “helped you start the day,” and toothpaste promising to “make you feel fresh like you just stepped outside.”

He wanted something direct, something actionable, something sacred in its simplicity. He had a deep, almost religious respect for routine, which he believed was the truest form of freedom. He once told a neighbor, “If you live your life according to someone else’s schedule, you’re not free. But if you follow your own, you’re just lonely. So give someone else a schedule and then follow it. That’s real liberty.”

Marvin had no idea how deeply his calendars would resonate. The first year, he printed five hundred copies, mostly to gift to friends and relations. By the third year, he was shipping thousands across the Midwest, responding to calls and faxes with clipped efficiency and an occasional anecdote about his late wife, who had liked to knit but never completed a scarf.

He never advertised, and he certainly never sought attention. His only ambition was to help people live better, tidier, more responsible lives. He never considered himself a spiritual leader, although a few church groups did try to claim him as a kind of secular saint. He declined all invitations to speak at conferences or appear on radio shows. “If it weren’t for the calendar,” he said once, “who would I be?”

No one in Midvale ever asked. They simply opened their mail each January, smiled at the familiar block letters, and followed the instructions.

THE annual report from the Bureau of Internal Resonance had just arrived, and already it was stirring unrest among the upper-middle tier of society. Though the document itself was a dry compendium of decibel measurements, harmonic frequencies, and subsonic anomalies, the implications were anything but. According to the findings, the average citizen emitted a baseline hum of 47.2 hertz, a figure slightly higher than the previous year’s 46.9 and a full three-tenths above the historically stable 46.5 recorded during the Great Silence of 1983. 

In the penthouse of 444 Harmonic Way, a man known only as Mr. Cull sat before a large, analog oscilloscope and let the numbers settle in. He had commissioned the report not for scientific curiosity, but because he had noticed a change in the air—a low, persistent pressure against the eardrums, like the world had been tuning itself all at once. His wife, Dr. Evangeline Cull, had stopped singing in the mornings. "It’s the resonance," she said. "Something’s shifting." She believed it was related to her work on the Urban Harmonics Initiative, a project meant to soothe restless cities through ambient sound therapy. Instead, it appeared to be making them louder.

By late afternoon, the streets of the city were buzzing. Not literally—though the bees were indeed more vocal—but in a more metaphorical sense. People spoke faster, moved quicker, and the usual urban murmur had become an aggressive chorus of overlapping conversations, car horns, and the kind of foot traffic that felt like it could vibrate glass. Even the pigeons had begun cooing in unison, and the trees in Central Park seemed to rustle in time with the pulse of the subway below. 

Mr. Cull left his penthouse just after sunset, carrying a small black device with a digital display and a pair of frequency filters. He moved through the city with a measured step, pausing occasionally to press the device to his ear and check the reading. Each block registered a slight uptick. By the time he reached the edge of the Financial District, where the old stock exchanges still hummed with outdated ticker tape and the ghosts of speculative deals past, the meter climbed to 48.1. 

He stopped at a bar near Wall Street, where the bartender, a former sound engineer turned mixologist, poured him a drink called “The Echo.” "People are getting antsy," the bartender said, adjusting the jukebox without playing it. "They say it’s the bass. Like someone turned up the world’s volume." 

Mr. Cull nodded, sipping slowly. He wasn’t sure what came next, only that whatever it was, it would be in tune.

A recent article in the Weekly Standard stated that we are suffering from a national crisis of silence. The writer blamed this phenomenon on a decline in religious observance and a rise in secular amnesia. I, for one, am not convinced. I believe the crisis stems from something else entirely—something far more mundane and infinitely more frustrating. It’s the proliferation of the word “literally” in the modern lexicon.

Once, “literally” meant precisely what it implied: in the exact manner described. If you said you were literally drowning in emails, it meant that water was entering your lungs. If someone was literally dancing with joy, you expected a tap shoe and a chorus line. But now, the word has mutated into a rhetorical device, a vague intensifier, a verbal sugar cube. It has become so common that it is barely noticed. And yet, it is the cause of countless misunderstandings, and perhaps more than a few nervous breakdowns.

I remember the first time I heard it used improperly. It was during a cocktail party in the East Village, where a guest claimed he was so hungry that he was literally eating dirt. We all laughed politely, assuming it was a joke. But the man insisted. He gestured wildly with a martini in one hand and a crumb-covered handkerchief in the other. The hostess, sensing danger, changed the record. We moved on to less volatile topics. Later, as I walked back to my apartment, I found myself wondering how many more people were out there claiming to live in literal hells and die of literal heartbreaks.

Since that evening, I’ve resolved to restore the word to its rightful place in the language. I’ve started a campaign—small at first, confined to dinner parties and book clubs. I correct people gently, pointing out the historical and semantic roots of the term. Some nod in agreement and promise to be more careful. Most roll their eyes and change the subject.

Still, I persist. I carry a small notebook with me, where I record misused instances of “literally.” I categorize them by context and frequency. Some entries are innocent, others more troubling. Last week, a neighbor described his divorce as “literally tearing him apart.” The phrase sent chills through me. I don’t know whether to comfort him or call an ambulance.

And yet, I remain hopeful. Change is slow, but it is coming. One corrected usage at a time, I believe we can reclaim our language from the fog of figurative excess.

"THE newest and final revision to the Comprehensive Manual of Ethical Decision-Making has just been approved by the International Committee of Moral Arbitration. The document is now sealed, laminated, and distributed via a satellite network that guarantees receipt by every citizen of the known civilized world—unless, of course, they have opted out, which only 0.007% have done, citing either religious exemption, philosophical anarchy, or a deep-seated distrust of laminated documents. The manual has 1,002 pages and weighs precisely 27.3 ounces, which coincidentally is the exact weight required to trigger the automated ethics scale embedded in every public desk, dining table, and even private nightstand. Once placed on the scale, the manual weighs nothing, which is one of its many paradoxes and perhaps the reason it is considered infallible. It contains no chapters, only numbered ethical dilemmas, each accompanied by a flowchart and a QR code that connects to an AI ethicist, who delivers a response in a calm, genderless voice and whose answers are binding under the Unified Code of Civil Discourse, unless challenged by a certified moral relativist, who must submit their counterarguments in triplicate to a tribunal of three retired schoolteachers, who are themselves bound by a smaller version of the manual. 

The manual's final entry is labeled "Ethical Dilemma #1001: What To Do If You Suspect That You Are Already Doing The Right Thing." The solution, as interpreted by the AI, is to continue doing so, but to keep a detailed log of your certainty in a font size no larger than 6-point to avoid appearing smug. The AI also recommends a daily dose of humility in pill form, administered sublingually. 

On the day of distribution, citizens are asked to recite the first stanza of the manual aloud, which reads: “In all things, consider the consequences, but only after accounting for the intentions, and never, ever, ignore the context.” This stanza is also tattooed onto the forearm of every newborn, in non-toxic ink, using a machine that applies the tattoo exactly seventeen seconds after birth, which studies have shown is the ideal time for imprinting moral frameworks. 

Meanwhile, the Committee has announced a new initiative: an annual awards ceremony celebrating individuals who have demonstrated exceptional moral consistency, defined as making the same ethically correct decision on at least three separate occasions. The first recipient will be announced in the spring, and the trophy is a transparent cube containing a live, breathing example of moral ambiguity, carefully bred in a lab and conditioned to respond only to perfectly phrased questions."

In 1987, the global consensus on the aesthetic merits of televised cooking shows reached a veritable tipping point, as evidenced by the seismic shift in viewer habits and the alarming dominance of Japanese-style culinary broadcasts. Industry analysts at *Media Matters Monthly* reported that the United States, long held in its gilded supremacy, had seen its market share in the genre plummet by nearly forty percent, with Tokyo, Osaka, and Kyoto jointly capturing the lion’s share of the world's hungry eyes.

These Japanese productions, marked by an almost religious reverence for precision and presentation, offered an experience more akin to a Zen ritual than mere sustenance. Each episode of *Shokudō no Kabe* featured not just recipes, but elaborate mise-en-scène—rice paper screens folding open to reveal pristine kitchens, the whisper of bamboo steam vents, and the precise angle at which a chef might place a single drop of soy on a silken tofu slice. These shows, it seemed, did not merely feed the body—they fed the soul with rhythm, order, and visual harmony.

By contrast, American cooking shows, despite their booming production numbers and celebrity chefs wielding spatulas like scepters, appeared increasingly like relics of a bygone era. The American format—loud, chaotic, and often suspiciously greasy—was still held up by stalwarts like Chef Tony Bigoli, whose signature catchphrase, “Boom! That’s a flavor bomb!” was both celebrated and quietly mocked in academic circles as emblematic of a culinary culture in decline.

The Japanese success was not accidental. According to Dr. Haruko Tanaka, a cultural semiotician at the Tokyo Institute of Culinary Discourse, the shows were steeped in centuries-old traditions of mindfulness and aesthetic control. “It’s not just about food,” she explained. “It’s about creating *wa*, a sense of balance and peace, in the act of eating itself.”

Meanwhile, in New York, at the headquarters of *Cooking America Today*, the network executives convened in a conference room filled with the smell of burnt garlic and regret. The ratings were in. Their flagship show had dropped by eleven points, and their new contestant-based format, *Sizzler Showdown*, had been called “a cacophonous mess” by *TV Critique Weekly*. The chairman, a man whose toupee had begun to take on a life of its own, stared out the window at the Hudson River and muttered something about reinvention and soul. Somewhere in Japan, a chef was just slicing an avocado in silence.

In 1983, the world finally accepted that happiness could be measured — not in smiles, nor in laughter, but in lumens. The breakthrough came quietly, like most paradigm shifts, from a lab in Kyoto where researchers discovered that sustained joy correlated almost perfectly with ambient lighting levels above 300 lux. Governments, corporations, and even churches rushed to adjust. The American Heart Association endorsed “lumense” as a substitute for exercise. Churches installed fiber-optic sun tunnels, and Wall Street brokers traded in stocks of natural light from the Andes and synthetic lumens produced by the Japanese firm Lumigami.

By 1985, the global happiness index was a standard, and the United States, with its vast deserts of sunlight and neon cities, led the world by a comfortable margin. But not for long. By 1987, a new challenger emerged: the Nordic Countries, armed with their own innovation — the Circadian Adjustment Lamp, or CAL. This device, resembling a desk lamp crossed with a satellite dish, adjusted the intensity and color of light throughout the day to mimic sunrise to sunset, and it did so with such precision that it induced a state of engineered well-being. Scandinavia’s average lumen score climbed to 532, surpassing even the sun-drenched U.S. Southwest.

In response, the American Department of Happiness — established in 1984, with an operating budget of $3.2 billion — convened an emergency summit in Denver, under the bright Colorado sun. The head of the department, Dr. Elmore T. Bright, a former advertising executive with a penchant for optimism and a wardrobe of fluorescent polos, addressed the assembled experts. “We must innovate,” he said. “We cannot let our children grow up believing that happiness comes from a cold white glow. Our happiness must be authentic.”

A new initiative was launched: the Luminous Living Movement, which encouraged citizens to embrace natural light. Homes were redesigned with skylights and glass walls, schools added solariums, and even prisons were fitted with transparent cells. A national ad campaign, starring a glowing Julia Roberts, urged citizens to “let happiness in.” For a while, it worked. The lumen scores ticked upward. But soon, the truth set in: the CALs were superior. Their light was softer, more human. The sun was too hot, too variable.

By 1990, the United States had fallen to fourth place in global happiness, surpassed by Thailand, which had developed the Happy Lantern, a rice-paper lantern infused with bioluminescent algae that glowed gently for eight hours at night. The American government, humiliated, tried to ban the import of foreign light devices. But the world had already changed. Light, it seemed, was the new religion. And the United States, for all its innovation, was now merely a follower in the illumination race.

THE newly announced launch of the V-770, a revolutionary all-purpose verbal assistant developed by Ventrilo, Inc., has sparked both excitement and skepticism across sectors ranging from corporate boardrooms to lonely bedrooms. Officially dubbed "The Voice of the Future," the V-770 is touted as capable of composing sonnets, filing taxes, conducting philosophical debates, and reciting your childhood bedtime stories—complete with accurate regional accents and emotionally nuanced pauses—while simultaneously managing your calendar, predicting your mood, and ordering groceries from stores you've never visited. According to Ventrilo’s glowing press release, the V-770 operates entirely on neural feedback, learning from your tone, cadence, and sighs to construct a profile of your personality so detailed it can anticipate your needs before you become aware of them. 

Unlike earlier models that required clunky hardware or intrusive app installations, the V-770 exists purely as an auditory presence. It lives in your ears via sleek, self-charging in-ear pods, and its voice—if it can be called that—shimmers between genders, accents, and inflections depending on the user's current emotional context. One user described it as "being comforted by a dream." Another said it felt “as though my best friend and my therapist had somehow merged into one entity.” 

Critics, however, have raised concerns about the device’s encroachment into private speech, its tendency to interrupt thoughts with unnervingly empathetic responses, and its inexplicable ability to mimic voices of deceased loved ones with uncanny accuracy. In a recent op-ed published in *The Lingual Review*, linguistics professor Dr. Eliza Varnum warned of a coming era in which the distinction between human and machine speech may become indistinguishable—and possibly unnecessary. "We are entering a phase of linguistic outsourcing," she wrote, "where meaning itself becomes curated by algorithm."

Early adopters, meanwhile, report that the experience is strangely intimate. Some users say they no longer feel the need to speak aloud, their sentences completing themselves inside the soft hum of the V-770’s always-listening presence. Others claim to hear the voice when they’re alone, even without the device active—a phenomenon Ventrilo has yet to address publicly.

In homes where the V-770 is installed, conversations begin to shift. People pause more often, weigh their words as if speaking to an unseen judge. The device, it seems, doesn’t just assist—it listens. It learns. And most unsettling of all, it remembers.

Some believed the [REDACTED]’s famed "Poached Scramble" was a clever loophole: neither strictly poached nor scrambled, but rather a semi-poached scramble with a translucent yolk core, folded with a ceremonial spoon by the club’s head cook, who was recently caught sleeping in a bread warmer. 

Inside the [REDACTED] Breakfast Club’s headquarters, a building that resembles a cross between a cathedral and a convenience store, the staff celebrated the win with a subdued fanfare of kazoos and a communal omelet made entirely from powdered eggs. Meanwhile, the [REDACTED] Breakfast Club, perennial runner-up and this year’s staunchest rival, held a press conference in a broom closet. In 1987, the advent of the “smart” greeting card sent ripples through the sentimental goods industry, long a sleepy backwater of commerce where sentimentality was packaged in cellophane and dispatched via postal service. The arrival of the Japanese-manufactured Feliz-AutoCard 2000, with its soft-focus holographic front cover and embedded microchip programmed to respond to ambient emotion, signaled a seismic shift. American card companies, still clambering for inspiration from the same pool of Victorian aphorisms and Christmas carols, watched helplessly as sales plummeted.

The Feliz-AutoCard 2000 worked by detecting minute facial expressions, vocal inflection, and skin conductivity, then selecting the most appropriate message and playback tone accordingly. If the recipient sighed upon opening it, the card played a slow, bluesy rendition of “If I Were a Rich Man,” followed by an elegantly phrased note in calligraphic print: *“Your burden is not invisible to me.”* If they smiled—or even tilted their head slightly—*“Hey, Good Looking!”* blared forth, and the message read: *“Let’s pretend this is the best day of the rest of our lives.”*

These weren’t just clever gimmicks; they were intimate encounters, tailored by algorithm. Cards were now more than vessels for sentiment—they were companions, confidants, even judges. And unlike humans, they were always calibrated for comfort.

In the U.S., Hallmark responded by hiring consultants from the same think tanks that once advised NASA on space shuttle morale. The result? The Hallmark EmpathX series, which, despite featuring a limited vocabulary and a tendency to misinterpret grief as “mild dissatisfaction,” failed to keep pace. One particularly confused model mistook a sneeze for a burst of joy and delivered a birthday message in a jubilant children’s choir.

Meanwhile, the Japanese kept iterating. The Feliz-AutoCard 3000 added a heartbeat sensor and GPS to personalize greetings with local weather forecasts and culturally specific metaphors. By the time the 4000 model reached shelves, it could generate handwritten-style letters in real time, complete with coffee stains and margin doodles, using a tiny ink-jet printer hidden in the corner.

In cafes across Tokyo and Kyoto, people sat with these cards open, reading the messages aloud, eyes glistening, not from nostalgia or friendship, but from the quiet, precise attention of something better than memory. Some said it was eerie. Others, a kind of mercy.

And somewhere, in a cluttered office in St. Louis, a Hallmark engineer quietly resigned, bought a one-way ticket to Osaka, and began learning the company song.

IN 1987, the global dominance of the 4a6170616eese-made espresso machine was so complete that even the most ardent supporters of the domestic brew began to admit it was, in essence, a lost cause. By that year, the 4a6170616eese had perfected a system where beans were selected, roasted, ground, and dispensed with such precision that each cup approximated, if not surpassed, the output of a master barista in Milan circa 1860. American cafés, once proud bastions of drip, percolation, and the occasional over-boiled pot, began quietly replacing their tired Mr. Coffee units with machines bearing names like “Nebula,” “Zenith,” and “Tengu”—machines that hummed like engines of a different age, smooth and quiet, with the kind of interface that looked more like a cockpit than a kitchen appliance.

The Japanese machines were sleek, efficient, and possessed a certain zen-like elegance that Americans, in their usual fashion, tried to mimic but could not replicate. The 4a6170616eese understood something fundamental about the ritual of coffee—its pacing, its pause, the reverence for the bean. Their machines incorporated sensors, timers, and pressure indicators that read not just the bean, but the mood of the person behind the counter. One of the most popular models, the Fujimoto 9000, had a programmable “Mood Brew” setting that could adjust the strength of the espresso depending on whether the user selected “Reflective,” “Stimulating,” or “Calm.”

Domestically, the response varied. Some manufacturers attempted to modernize the traditional American drip, adding timers, auto-shutoffs, and a “Bold Mode” that mostly just burnt the beans more thoroughly. Others tried to rebrand the French press as a “manual espresso alternative,” though this only confused more people than it enlightened. A few desperate companies attempted fusion models, hybridizing the drip with the Italian stovetop moka pot, but the result was generally underwhelming and slightly alarming to baristas.

The shift was more than aesthetic—it was philosophical. The 4a6170616eese espresso machine represented not just a better brew, but a different way of thinking about the act of making and consuming it. Where the American machine was a utilitarian tool, the Japanese machine was a partner in ritual, a kind of silent collaborator in the art of drinking consciousness.

By 1989, the last of the major U.S. brands had exited the market, unable to keep pace with the relentless efficiency and quiet revolution of the 4a6170616eese brew. Coffee shops began to rename themselves “Espresso Houses.” Baristas studied abroad. The future of the bean had clearly been written in Kanji—and it was brewed under pressure.

IN 1986, the United States successfully rebranded grief into a multi-billion-dollar industry. It began, as many such things do, with a congressional bill—HR 2817—commonly known as the “Emotionally Tax-Deductible Assets Act.” Ostensibly passed to assist grieving families in processing loss, the legislation allowed citizens to write off any expenses incurred in the immediate aftermath of a death, including, but not limited to, funerals, sympathy flowers, counseling sessions, and even the cost of a new television in a home deemed “emotionally empty” following a loss. By the end of the first quarter, Americans had deducted over $11 billion in "grief-related expenditures," and analysts predicted a full-blown boom.  

The funeral home sector saw an immediate uptick. Traditional wakes became “curated mourning experiences,” featuring ambient music, artisanal tea bars, and curated photo slideshows set to user-selected soundtracks. The CEO of Dignity Plus Memorials, a leading provider in the field, announced at a Wall Street conference that the company would soon be offering “grief-themed travel packages”—all-expenses-paid trips for surviving family members to locations meaningful to the deceased, complete with guided reflection circles and optional group drumming.  

At the same time, the mental health industry capitalized on the new tax code by introducing “grief productivity” as a core brand promise. Therapists now billed in “emotional units,” where a full hour of crying and recollection counted as 1.5 sessions. Counseling centers across the country adopted a streamlined, assembly-line approach: one room for denial, another for bargaining, a third for depression, with a waiting area where clients could collect their tax receipts upon completion. Grief coaching became a booming niche, with influencers offering daily 5-minute guided “acceptance sprints” on platforms like YouTube and LinkedIn.  

Meanwhile, insurance companies expanded coverage to include what they termed “preventative mourning.” Policies now covered “anticipated grief,” allowing policyholders to deduct expenses like pre-funeral planning and “emotional maintenance fees” for those anticipating loss due to age, illness, or geographic proximity to areas with high mortality rates. One insurer, BlueHeart Life, launched a controversial campaign promising “tax-free sorrow” through life settlements and accelerated depreciation of loved ones.  

By October, critics were calling it a moral hazard. Grief, once a private, unpredictable burden, had become a scheduled expense, a commodity to be managed, optimized, and, when necessary, postponed. Some worried about inflation—would the rising cost of sympathy bouquets affect the Consumer Price Index? Others questioned the ethics of a system where the dead could be leveraged for economic gain.  

Still, for the American consumer, HR 2817 was a revelation. As one grieving widow told a reporter for *Forbes*: “I’m not crying anymore—I’m investing.”

The United States won the International Championship of National Identity for the fourth consecutive year, despite the fact that, as one observer noted, “the trophy they brought wasn’t actually theirs.” The ceremony, held in the Grand Hall of Global Symbols in Vienna, featured a parade of flags, a synchronized flash mob of national anthems performed by trained volunteers, and a keynote speech by the U.S. delegation’s lead mascot—a six-foot-tall eagle in a business suit who spoke in short bursts of clipped, triumphant phrases. “We believe in the idea,” he declared, “not the icon.”

Back in Washington, the response was muted. The White House did not issue a press release, nor did it host a victory party. Instead, the President was seen quietly revising the national anthem, adding an extra verse that included the words “unbought,” “unchained,” and “untweetable.” His advisors debated the significance of the change. Some saw it as poetic. Others thought it was redundant.

In fact, the U.S. had not truly “won” the Championship in decades. The contest had evolved from a celebration of authenticity into a contest of irony, a kind of reverse pageant where the most aware of their own constructedness rose to the top. Canada, perennial runner-up, once known for maple syrup and hockey, had rebranded entirely as “The Nation Formerly Known As Canada.” Brazil had entered under the alias “Tropical Melancholia,” a move that confused the judges but won the crowd.

This year, the real competition had taken place in the margins. South Korea submitted a video entry titled *Self-Portrait in Ten Mirrors*, featuring a rotating cast of identical androids reciting the Korean constitution in unison, while Japan presented *Unbranding Nihon*, a performance art piece in which citizens voluntarily erased their national symbols from public spaces using industrial-grade erasers.

The U.S. had entered nothing. It simply showed up, as it always did, in whatever form it had assumed that week. On this particular day, it arrived looking like a vintage diner, complete with neon sign reading “AMERICA’S BEST BITES (NOT ACTUALLY AMERICAN).” Inside, journalists were handed menus with options like “Freedom Wings” and “Liberty Mac ‘n’ Cheese,” though no one ate. They took pictures instead.

Later, in a backstage interview, the eagle in a suit was asked why the U.S. seemed so certain of itself. He blinked slowly and replied, “Identity is a performance. The key is to perform convincingly while knowing you’re faking it.” Someone laughed. It was unclear who.

The trophy, by the way, is currently on display at the Smithsonian, where it has been labeled *Untitled (Won by Accident)*.

THE HISTORICAL SOCIETY OF AMERICAN EMBARGOS is pleased to announce the inaugural induction of the Embargo Hall of Fame, a prestigious new initiative aimed at honoring the most influential, creatively enforced, and economically transformative trade restrictions in U.S. history. Following a rigorous vetting process overseen by a panel of eleven Nobel Prize winners in Economics, two former U.S. ambassadors to the Banana Republic of Nowhere, and the current head of the International League of Embargo Enthusiasts, the first inductees represent a diverse array of geopolitical contexts and moral ambiguities. Among the honorees is the 1917 Grain Embargo Against the Austro-Hungarian Empire, which led to the accidental creation of the first commercially viable gluten-free bread and the rise of a minor Austrian composer whose only surviving symphony was titled “Inflation in C Minor.” Also recognized is the 1952–1953 Steel Embargo, which not only halted tank production in the Eastern Bloc but inadvertently gave birth to the modern skyscraper through a surge in demand for iron-replacement materials. The 1979 Oil Embargo, naturally, takes center stage in this year’s ceremony, celebrated for its role in the invention of the hybrid electric vehicle, the expansion of the national highway snack culture, and a significant increase in the popularity of jogging as a patriotic duty. Honorees will be immortalized in a new bronze-relief mural at the Society’s headquarters in Alexandria, Virginia—though recent discussions have suggested that marble, for its superior oil-resistance, might be the better choice. The Hall of Fame’s founding chairman, Dr. Harold Pynchon III, expressed his enthusiasm during a private luncheon at the Willard Intercontinental Hotel: “These embargoes,” he declared, “are not merely acts of economic warfare; they are cultural catalysts, industrial accelerants, and sometimes, simply, the best ideas we’ve ever had.” Indeed, the Society’s archives indicate that 67% of all post-embargo patents filed between 1945 and 2000 originated from industries destabilized by prior sanctions. As the world continues to grapple with the complex interplay of globalization and isolationism, the Embargo Hall of Fame offers a lighthearted but historically grounded reminder that even the most stubborn barriers can spark innovation, unity—and a surprisingly rich legacy. The induction ceremony is scheduled for November 11th, coinciding with the centennial of the Embargo on Tea Imports from the British-controlled Indian Subcontinent, an event that many now consider the unofficial birthdate of the American iced coffee industry.

In 1989, the global dominance of the Swiss-engineered mousetrap reached its apex when the International Mouse Control Association (IMCA), in a unanimous vote, awarded the Model Z-87 "Trap of the Century." The accolade was delivered during the annual IMCA gala in Basel, where delegates from sixty-two countries gathered to witness the momentous occasion. The trap, a sleek, minimalist contraption constructed entirely of tempered glass and a single springless mechanism powered by solar energy, captured rodents with a silent efficiency that left traditional snap-trap manufacturers scrambling to justify their place in the modern world. 

The Z-87 did not kill. It did not maim. It simply contained. Its transparent chamber, embedded with a soft LED glow and a faint melody composed by a Kyoto-based ambient music collective, lured mice inside with an irresistible blend of warmth and serenity. Once inside, the mouse would often sit up and groom itself, as if content with its fate, its tiny whiskers twitching in appreciation of the design. 

American competitors, who had relied for decades on rusted steel jaws and bait made of peanut butter or cheese (both of which, as the USDA had recently confirmed, had no proven effectiveness against urban Norway rats), began to fold. A spokesperson for the National Pest Control Association of the United States released a statement claiming, “Switzerland’s victory is not a defeat for the spirit of American ingenuity—it is a reminder that even our finest ideas can be improved upon through international collaboration.” Meanwhile, in Basel, a new apprenticeship program was launched under the banner of “Swiss Craftsmanship for a Humane World,” with students learning to engrave motivational phrases onto the inner walls of the traps in Latin and Mandarin. 

By 1991, the Model Z-87 had been adapted for domestic pets. Variants appeared for cats, dogs, and even parrots—each one featuring custom lighting and soothing sounds tailored to the species. Dogs, for instance, preferred a low-frequency hum reminiscent of distant thunderstorms, while parrots responded best to recordings of rainforest chatter mixed with the soft crackle of a campfire. The traps were rebranded as “Enrichment Units,” and their purpose, according to the updated IMCA mission statement, was no longer extermination but enrichment—offering creatures of all kinds a brief respite from the chaos of existence. 

And so, in the basement of the old Johnson house on Maple Street in suburban Des Moines, a field mouse found its way into the Z-87 model sitting beneath the furnace. He blinked at the light, then at the ceiling, where a single drop of dust floated lazily through the beam. Then he curled up, and everything became quiet.

IN 1985, the world awoke to the revelation that the United States had, without prior announcement or congressional approval, begun training its national basketball team in the art of diplomacy. The revelation came not from the State Department, which had maintained its usual opacity, nor from the Olympics Committee, which claimed to have "had nothing to do with it," but from an unlikely source: a junior analyst in the Pentagon’s Office of Unconventional Strategic Affairs. His name was Lieutenant Randy Flick, and he had stumbled upon the truth while reclassifying old files under a directive titled “Operation Hoops.”

At the time, everyone assumed the U.S. men’s team was simply preparing for the World Championships in Melbourne, a routine exhibition of athletic excellence and capitalist optimism. But as Flick began poring over budget requests labeled things like “Ambassadorially Appropriate Sneakers” and “Diplomatic Court Dimensions,” it became clear that something far more elaborate was afoot. The team wasn’t just practicing layups anymore—they were studying the history of the League of Nations, memorizing the names of every African ambassador to the UN, and learning how to pivot smoothly from a three-pointer to a three-point speech on human rights in Tibet.

The training, it turned out, had been going on for three years. The first sign of trouble had been the sudden and inexplicable inclusion of two former diplomats—now retired and slightly corpulent—to the team’s regular scrimmage sessions. At first dismissed as consultants, their roles soon expanded to include impromptu simulations of Cold War summit meetings staged on portable hardwood floors in the middle of Nevada’s desert. These exercises, complete with mock press conferences and live translators, were said to be crucial for developing "soft-hand ball handling" and "multilateral footwork."

By the end of the summer, rumors swirled. The Chinese delegation had reportedly declined an invitation to a practice game, citing “ethical concerns about the militarization of sport.” Meanwhile, members of Congress raised questions about the $12 million allocated for “basketball infrastructure” that appeared to fund neither rims nor dribbles. When pressed, the White House responded with a statement that read, in part, “Our team plays not for victory, but for understanding. The net, after all, is woven globally.”

It was a strange time to be American. The Cold War was heating up again in the newsreels, but in the gym, something else was in play—a quieter, subtler form of soft power, hoisted by ankles and released like a well-timed pass. And as the players stepped onto the plane to Australia, their jerseys stitched with stars and stripes and slogans like “Pass, Don’t Clash,” no one—not even Randy Flick—could predict whether they would come back with gold medals or just the ghost of a handshake.

Industry insiders were stunned. For decades, the annual competition had been a genteel affair, marked by slow, incremental improvements in motor efficiency, ergonomic design, and the ability to quietly vacuum under the furniture of the world’s leaders. But the VX-4000 had arrived with a bang—or rather, with a whisper. Its proprietary "SilentSwoop" technology allowed it to operate at zero decibels, a claim many doubted until the French delegation at the awards ceremony presented a video showing the VX-4000 cleaning the Louvre’s marble floors while a flock of pigeons inexplicably refused to move.

In [REDACTED] City, where the VX-4000 was assembled in a factory that once manufactured typewriters for the pre-digital era, the news was met with civic euphoria. Local children painted murals of the VX-4000 on the sides of houses, and a pop band released a ballad titled “Whisper Me Clean,” which peaked at #43 on the charts. Meanwhile, the conglomerate’s stock price surged by 147 percent overnight, prompting one analyst to note, “It’s like if the Mona Lisa suddenly started filing her own income taxes.”

But the real intrigue lay in the VX-4000’s rumored secret feature: a built-in AI, allegedly trained on centuries of etiquette manuals and interior design blogs, capable of determining which areas of the home needed vacuuming based on the emotional state of the homeowner. Whether this claim was true remained unclear, but the possibility had already sparked a minor philosophical debate in academic circles about whether appliances could possess agency—and if so, how that might redefine human responsibility in the home.

THE 1992 INT'L CHAMPIONSHIP FOR HUMANISTIC OPTIMISM IS NOW OFFICIALLY OPEN FOR ENTRIES. The International League for Positive Projections (ILPP), based in a repurposed convent in Luxembourg, has extended its deadline until October 1st for submissions from hopeful participants across the globe. This is the twenty-seventh year the ILPP has hosted the event, which, unlike the Olympics or the World Cup, requires no athletic prowess, no linguistic fluency, and no knowledge of anything invented after 1900. Instead, contestants must demonstrate their ability—through written statement, performance art, or a compelling PowerPoint presentation—of maintaining, in the face of historical adversity, a steadfast and believable optimism. This year’s theme, as announced by the league’s president, Dr. Helga Vinter, in her keynote speech titled “Hope is Not a Luxury Item,” is “Optimism in the Midst of Moderate Collapse.” 

Last year’s champion, a retired librarian from Sofia named Mira Stancheva, won with a twenty-minute lecture on the enduring charm of Soviet-era cassettes and the moral superiority of state-sponsored bread rations. Her final slide, displayed on an overhead projector and accompanied by a lullaby sung in Bulgarian, read: “If we can survive the eighties, we can survive anything.” She received her trophy—a bronze laurel wreath mounted on a yogurt cup—and a lifetime supply of optimism-themed literature from the ILPP Press. 

This year’s competition is expected to be fierce, despite the relatively low stakes. Reports from regional qualifiers indicate a surge in entries from Eastern Europe, Scandinavia, and the American Midwest. A former dairy farmer from Iowa, citing the collapse of his family business and the rise of corn-based ethanol, is reportedly submitting a multimedia installation titled “Milk Again, Someday.” A collective from Helsinki has proposed a kinetic sculpture involving rotating Finnish saunas and a recurring refrain of “It gets better!” played on kantele.

The ILPP has seen its share of controversy over the years. Critics claim the event is frivolous, a joke disguised as a contest. Others accuse it of being a front for multinational corporations seeking to monetize hope through sponsored optimism kits. The league dismisses these allegations as sour grapes, noting that even the most hardened pessimists must occasionally feel a flicker of something resembling optimism. “After all,” says Dr. Vinter in the press release, “we’re all in this together. Even when it’s falling apart.” 

And fall apart it will, inevitably. But the championship continues, as does the effort to keep the lights on, the music playing, and the belief in the next possible step.

The United States Navy announced yesterday the cancellation of its experimental program to teach dolphins how to navigate nuclear submarines using whale songs. Codenamed Operation Sirensong, the initiative had been in development for over a decade under the auspices of the Oceanographic Research and Tactical Submersion Unit, or ORTSU, a division of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency with jurisdiction extending only to the Atlantic and Gulf coasts. According to an unsigned press release obtained by the *Washington Sentinel*, the project’s termination comes “as part of a broader reassessment of interspecies communication in the context of national defense and ecological ethics.”

The press release claims that the dolphins, trained to recognize and replicate complex patterns of Morse code embedded within humpback whale ballads, had made "limited but notable progress." However, officials noted concerns about the ethical implications of subjecting sentient marine life to what one anonymous source described as “a kind of underwater cognitive militarization.” The dolphins, bred in captivity from genetically diverse stock sourced primarily from the Florida Keys and the Gulf of Mexico, were reportedly conditioned to respond not just to specific melodies but to entire symphonic structures, including key modulations and rhythmic shifts, in order to encode and decode operational orders.

Despite these achievements, the project faced criticism from both within and outside the Department of Defense. Environmental groups accused the Navy of exploiting marine life in the name of dubious technological advancement, citing previous controversies over sonar testing and its effects on cetacean populations. Meanwhile, internal memos revealed that certain senior officers harbored philosophical objections to the notion of using non-human intelligence to execute classified tasks. “There is,” wrote one such officer in a 2009 memo, “a disquieting asymmetry in our willingness to weaponize animals while pretending not to.”

With the program shuttered, the dozen trained bottlenose dolphins are scheduled for relocation to a privately funded research sanctuary in the Azores, where they will presumably spend the remainder of their lives in a controlled environment listening to music composed solely for their auditory enjoyment. As for the Navy, it is turning its attention to a new initiative—Project Sonar-Brain—which seeks to map the neural pathways of midshipmen using echolocation simulators and ambient noise generated by decommissioned submarines. Whether this marks a true shift toward ethical innovation, or merely a new kind of militarized curiosity, remains to be heard.
